passage:
Tuesday
Mohit got 4 out of 20 in his spelling test. I saw it in his bag. At dinner I said, "Papa, guess who got FOUR?" and laughed. Papa looked at me, and I thought he'd say I was the good one. But he just rubbed his eyes and said, "Not now, Divyansh."
Later I told Mummy that Mohit hid the test. I thought she would be pleased with me. She just sighed.
Mohit didn't talk to me all evening. When I went to sleep he had turned his back. He whispered, "I'll never tell you anything again."
I thought I'd feel like the winner. I don't.
Divyansh

qa.q: What did Mohit get in his spelling test?
qa.a: He got 4 out of 20.

qa.q: What did Divyansh want when telling on Mohit?
qa.a: Divyansh wanted Papa and Mummy to see Divyansh as the good one and be pleased.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do next time he finds out about Mohit's mistake?
qa.a: He could keep it private or even offer to help with spelling, instead of mocking or reporting, so Mohit can trust Divyansh again.

qa.q: How does Mohit feel after the dinner?
qa.a: He feels hurt and betrayed, which is why he turned his back and said he'd never tell Divyansh anything again.

grounding: It shows a child mocking a brother's failure and telling on him to win a parent's approval, leaving a tired parent and a brother with a real grievance.

passage: Evening in the village, and Sharmila had just come back from the fields, her feet dusty and her back aching. Before she could sit, Minakshi ran up. "Amma! Madhu broke the pot at the well and he fell in the mud, he looked so silly!" She laughed and flapped her arms like him falling. "And he didn't do his homework!" Madhu stood behind the door, his face red. Sharmila closed her eyes. "Minakshi, enough." Minakshi's smile faded. She had expected Amma to say, good girl for telling. Madhu glared at her and went to the back of the house. He didn't call her for their usual game of stones that night.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say Madhu broke?
qa.a: She said he broke the pot at the well.

qa.q: What did Minakshi expect when she told Amma?
qa.a: She expected Amma to praise her as a good girl for telling, wanting her mother's favour.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Mocking and reporting Madhu only tired Amma and hurt Madhu; Minakshi could say sorry to Madhu, and Amma could later talk to each child calmly and separately.

qa.q: How does Madhu feel after being mocked in front of Amma?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and angry, so he glares at his sister and skips their usual game of stones.

grounding: It illustrates a child mocking her brother and telling on him to gain adult favour, which only wearies the parent and gives the brother a real grievance.

subtype: Stage 4: The middle child's or younger one's view [Receiver]
passage:
Saturday
Hrithik bhaiya and Arush bhaiya were playing cricket on the terrace again. I asked to play. Hrithik said, "You can be the fielder who fetches the ball." That's not playing! That's being a servant!
Then they made a secret club with a password and wouldn't tell me. Arush said I'm too small to understand.
I told Mamma it was unfair. She said, "Teju, they're older, let them be." Nobody listens to me because I'm the youngest girl. I can bowl better than Arush, actually. I just want them to say, "Teju, you're good, come play properly."
Tejaswini

qa.q: What job did Hrithik offer Teju in the cricket game?
qa.a: He offered her the job of fielder who fetches the ball.

qa.q: What does Teju really want from her brothers?
qa.a: She wants them to take her seriously and admire her, like saying she's good and letting her play properly, not just tolerate her.

qa.q: How could Mamma respond at this stage?
qa.a: She could listen to Teju's feelings and gently ask the brothers to give her a real turn, instead of saying "let them be."

qa.q: What would change if the brothers let Teju bowl?
qa.a: Teju would feel included and respected, and the brothers might discover she really can bowl well. 🙂

grounding: It shows the youngest sister feeling bossed and shut out of her older brothers' games, wanting to be taken seriously, not merely tolerated.

subtype: Stage 4: The middle child's or younger one's view [Receiver]
passage: Behind the house in the small town of Dharwad, Sunaina and her friends were playing hopscotch with chalk squares on the road. Nandini, seven, stood at the edge with her own chalk. "Can I play, akka?" Sunaina, eleven, didn't even look. "You'll mess it up. Go draw." The big girls laughed. Nandini drew a small square alone and hopped in it, again and again. When Appa came home, she ran to him. "Akka never lets me play! It's not fair!" "She's older, she has her own friends," Appa said, patting her head. Nandini went quiet. She didn't want a pat. She wanted Sunaina to say, "Come, Nandu, your turn."

qa.q: What game were Sunaina and her friends playing?
qa.a: They were playing hopscotch with chalk squares on the road.

qa.q: What did Nandini want when she ran to Appa?
qa.a: She wanted someone to take her feelings seriously, and most of all she wanted Sunaina to include her and give her a turn.

qa.q: What could Appa do to help at this stage?
qa.a: He could listen to why Nandini feels left out and ask Sunaina to give her a real turn, rather than brushing it off with a pat.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see her little sister joining in?
qa.a: Sunaina may see her as a nuisance who spoils the game in front of friends, not realising how much Nandini looks up to her.

grounding: It illustrates a younger sister who feels bossed and left out of her older sister's games and wants to be taken seriously, not just tolerated.

passage:
Monday. Jahnavi and Rafiq both showed Ma their drawings. Ma used to say whose was better. This time she said, "Jahnavi, you worked so long on the shading. Rafiq, look how brave those colours are." Both grinned.
Wednesday. They argued over the swing. Ma stayed at the window, watching, and did not step in. After some shouting, Rafiq said, "Five pushes each?" Jahnavi agreed.
Saturday. Rafiq climbed too high on the wall. Ma came out at once and helped him down. Later, when Jahnavi's kite tangled, Rafiq helped her fix it without anyone asking. Ma noticed they hadn't said "I'm better" all week.

qa.q: What deal did Rafiq suggest for the swing?
qa.a: He suggested five pushes each.

qa.q: What does Rafiq helping with the kite unasked suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt less need to compete with Jahnavi and more willing to help her, now that he isn't being compared.

qa.q: What did Ma do differently that helped?
qa.a: She praised each child's own effort, let them solve the swing quarrel themselves and stepped in only when Rafiq was unsafe on the wall.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi experience her mother's new way of praising?
qa.a: Jahnavi likely feels seen for their own work, like the shading, so there is no need to beat Rafiq to feel good.

grounding: It shows a parent praising each child's own effort, letting them settle small quarrels and stepping in only for safety, easing rivalry.

passage:
Vaibhav, you asked why I never say which of you cousins is the cleverest. Sit, I'll tell you. When your Papa and his brother were small, I always compared. "Look at Suresh's marks, why can't you?" They fought all the time, over everything. One day a teacher told me, "Praise each one for what he does." So I tried. I told your Papa his handwriting was careful, and Suresh that he was a good runner. When they quarrelled over small things, I let them sort it out, and only stepped in if someone might get hurt. Slowly, they stopped trying to beat each other. Now they talk every day.
— your Indu Dadi

qa.q: What did Indu Dadi praise Vaibhav's Papa for?
qa.a: She praised his careful handwriting.

qa.q: How did Indu Dadi feel about her old habit of comparing?
qa.a: She seems to regret it, since it made her sons fight over everything, which is why she changed.

qa.q: What approach did Indu Dadi switch to, and why did it work?
qa.a: She praised each son for his own strengths and let them solve small quarrels, so they no longer had to compete for her approval.

qa.q: How might Suresh have felt when his mother stopped comparing?
qa.a: He probably felt less pressure and more valued for his running, and less need to beat his brother.

grounding: It illustrates a parent who stops comparing, praises each child's own strengths and lets small quarrels be settled by them, so the siblings stop competing.

passage:
Come here, Norbu, let me tell you about your cousins Ira and Pema. They fought like cats at home, over the remote, the window seat, everything. But last week I took them to the park in Gangtok. A big boy pushed Pema off the slide and called him a baby. Before I could stand up, Ira was there, hands on hips. "Don't you touch my brother!" And Pema, still sniffling, stood behind her and shouted, "Yeah! She's my sister!" The big boy walked off. On the way home they held hands. That night, they fought over the blanket again. I laughed. That is siblings, Norbu. They fight each other, and then they fight for each other.
— your grandmother, Mola

qa.q: Where did Mola take Ira and Pema?
qa.a: She took them to the park in Gangtok.

qa.q: What does Pema shouting "She's my sister!" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows that despite their fights, he feels proud and loyal to Ira and wanted to stand with her.

qa.q: How could Mola or the parents build on the loyalty seen at the park?
qa.a: They could tell Ira and Pema what they noticed and praise them for standing up for each other, while still letting them sort out squabbles like the blanket fight themselves.

qa.q: What might the big boy have made of the two siblings standing together?
qa.a: He probably expected an easy target and did not count on a sister and brother standing up together, so he gave up and walked off.

grounding: It shows a grandparent seeing two quarrelling siblings defend each other against an outsider, showing that rivalry and loyalty live together.

passage: The Diwali fair was so crowded that Dadi could barely see over the heads, and she kept losing sight of Avni and Kashish near the rides. At home the two had fought all morning over who got the red lantern. Now Dadi spotted them by the merry-go-round. An older boy had cut in front of Kashish and shoved him. Avni stepped right between them. "Don't push my brother. He was here first." Kashish stood beside her, chin up. The older boy muttered and moved back. When Dadi finally reached them, they were climbing onto the same horse, laughing. Dadi smiled. The red lantern could wait.

qa.q: What had Avni and Kashish fought over that morning?
qa.a: They had fought over who got the red lantern.

qa.q: How can you tell Kashish felt braver with Avni beside him?
qa.a: He stood beside her with his chin up after she stepped between him and the older boy.

qa.q: What would you tell parents who worry about constant sibling fights?
qa.a: Fights are normal, and the same siblings can defend each other when it counts, so it helps to nurture that loyalty rather than only focusing on the quarrels.

qa.q: How does Dadi see the moment at the merry-go-round?
qa.a: She sees the loyalty beneath their rivalry and feels glad, smiling as they ride the same horse.

grounding: It illustrates a grandparent watching quarrelling siblings stand up for each other against an outsider, showing loyalty growing alongside rivalry.

passage:
"Vaibhav, time to go home now."
"No! Swing!"
"One more push, then home."
Yamini gave one push. "Okay, all done."
"No! No! Swing!"
Vaibhav's face crumpled. His hands gripped the chains. His legs went stiff.
"Come, baby. Mumma's here."
"Nooo!"
He started to cry, big tears rolling down.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav say when told it was time to go home?
qa.a: Vaibhav said, "No! Swing!"

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when his face crumpled?
qa.a: He felt sad and angry about leaving, and he could not handle the wish to stay.

qa.q: What could Yamini do at this first moment?
qa.a: She could name his feeling, like "You love the swing," and give a simple warning before leaving, staying calm as he cries.

qa.q: How might Yamini be feeling as Vaibhav starts crying?
qa.a: She may feel tired or worried about the scene, but she can see he is only little and upset.

grounding: It shows a toddler told it is time to leave the park who cannot manage the wish to stay, so his face crumples, his body stiffens and he cries.

passage:
Babysitter's note, Thursday.
At the park at five, I told Uday it was time to go. He was in the sandpit. He looked up, and his lip started to shake. He held his spade tight. When I held out my hand, he went stiff all over and threw his head back. Then he cried loudly. I knelt and said, "You wanted to stay. It's hard to go."
— Harsha

qa.q: Where was Uday when it was time to go?
qa.a: Uday was in the sandpit.

qa.q: What did Uday's shaking lip show?
qa.a: It showed he was getting upset and frustrated at having to leave.

qa.q: What did Harsha do that helped?
qa.a: Harsha knelt and named Uday's feeling, which helps a toddler feel understood.

qa.q: How might Uday's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Harsha stayed kind and calm when Uday got upset.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler told to leave the park who cannot manage wanting to stay, so his lip shakes, his body stiffens and he cries.

passage: The supermarket in Nairobi was busy. Wanjiru said no to the sweets. Kamau, two, dropped to the floor. He screamed. He kicked his legs and arched his back. He threw his shoe. Wanjiru knelt. "Kamau, listen, please..." He screamed louder. People turned to look. Her friend Mina, pushing the trolley, whispered, "He can't hear anything right now." Wanjiru nodded and stayed close, waiting.

qa.q: What did Kamau throw?
qa.a: He threw his shoe.

qa.q: Why could Kamau not listen to his mother?
qa.a: He was too upset to listen or reason, because a toddler's brain cannot calm itself down yet.

qa.q: What choice did Wanjiru make that helped?
qa.a: She stopped trying to talk him out of it and stayed close, waiting for the storm to pass.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru feel with people turning to look?
qa.a: She may feel embarrassed and stressed, but Mina's words help her stay calm.

grounding: It shows a toddler at the peak of a tantrum, dropping, screaming, kicking, throwing and arching, unable to listen or reason.

passage: I'm Manjula, from the flat downstairs. Yesterday in the lobby I saw Devika's little boy, Kanha, lying on the floor. He was screaming and kicking. He threw his toy car at the wall. Devika was saying, "Kanha, stop, listen to Mumma." He only screamed more and arched his back. I don't think he could hear her at all. Devika moved the toy car away and sat near him.

qa.q: What did Kanha throw at the wall?
qa.a: He threw his toy car at the wall.

qa.q: Why does Manjula think Kanha could not hear his mother?
qa.a: He was in the middle of a big storm of feeling, screaming more and arching his back, too upset to listen.

qa.q: What did Devika do that was helpful?
qa.a: She moved the toy car away to keep things safe and sat near Kanha instead of arguing with him.

qa.q: How does the scene look to Manjula?
qa.a: Manjula sees a toddler overwhelmed by feelings and a mother trying hard to cope.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler at the height of a tantrum, screaming, kicking and throwing, unable to listen or reason.

subtype: Stage 3: Caregiver's stress and choice point [Observer]
passage: I'm Kamal. I run the tea stall at the bus stop. Yesterday a young mother, Arohi, was waiting with her little boy. He threw himself on the ground, screaming. The bus was late. People stared. One man said loudly, "Just give him a slap." Arohi's face went red. She looked like she might shout. Then she took a breath, crouched beside him and kept him away from the road. She stayed calm.

qa.q: Where is Kamal's tea stall?
qa.a: Kamal runs it at the bus stop.

qa.q: How can you tell Arohi felt embarrassed and stressed?
qa.a: Her face went red when people stared and the man spoke loudly, and she looked like she might shout.

qa.q: Which choice did Arohi make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She chose to breathe, crouch beside her son and keep him safe from the road, which is harder than shouting but helps him calm down.

qa.q: How might Arohi see the man's remark?
qa.a: It probably added to her embarrassment and pressure, making staying calm even harder.

grounding: It shows a caregiver feeling embarrassed and stressed with strangers watching, choosing to stay calm and safe nearby instead of shouting or giving in.

subtype: Stage 3: Caregiver's stress and choice point [Observer]
passage:
Monday. At the mall, little Chintu screamed on the floor. Anand shouted, "Stop it now!" Chintu screamed louder. Disha watched Anand's jaw tighten.
Thursday. Chintu screamed for a balloon. Anand, tired, bought it. Chintu stopped, but Disha saw him watching his father closely.
Sunday. Another storm at the park. Anand looked at Disha, breathed slowly, knelt nearby and waited quietly. Chintu calmed down.

qa.q: What did Chintu scream for on Thursday?
qa.a: He screamed for a balloon.

qa.q: What does Anand's tight jaw on Monday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt angry and embarrassed by the tantrum in public.

qa.q: Which of Anand's three choices worked best, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm and waiting nearby on Sunday worked best, because it neither frightened Chintu nor taught him that screaming gets things.

qa.q: How might Disha see Anand's change over the week?
qa.a: Disha may feel relieved and proud to see him choose the harder, calmer way.

grounding: It illustrates a caregiver's choice point during tantrums, shouting, giving in, or staying calm nearby, with calm being hardest and most useful.

passage:
"Chetan, it's bath time."
"NO!" Chetan threw himself down, kicking.
Saurabh knelt down. His voice went low. "You are upset. I am here."
"No bath! No!"
Saurabh quietly moved the toy truck away from Chetan's feet.
"I'm right here."
Chetan screamed and kicked. Saurabh didn't argue. He just waited, close by.
After a while, Chetan's screams got smaller.

qa.q: What did Saurabh move away from Chetan's feet?
qa.a: He moved the toy truck away from Chetan's feet.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel when it was bath time?
qa.a: He felt angry and upset because he did not want a bath.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that helped Chetan most?
qa.a: He knelt, spoke in a low voice, kept things safe and waited without arguing, showing Chetan that big feelings can pass.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel with Saurabh staying close?
qa.a: Even while screaming, he may feel safe knowing Saurabh is still there. 🤍

grounding: It shows a caregiver kneeling, saying you are upset, I am here in a low voice, moving objects aside and waiting without argument.

passage:
Daycare note, Friday.
At nap time Omkar (2) had a big tantrum. He lay on the mat, crying and hitting the floor. I knelt near him. I said softly, "You are upset. I am here." I moved the water bottle and blocks away. I did not argue. I just stayed. Slowly his crying got softer. He crawled to me. 🤍
— Hemant, teacher

qa.q: Where did Omkar lie during his tantrum?
qa.a: He lay on the mat.

qa.q: What does Omkar crawling to Hemant show?
qa.a: It shows Omkar felt safe and wanted comfort once the storm eased.

qa.q: Why did Hemant's way work?
qa.a: Hemant stayed close, kept things safe and did not argue, so Omkar learned his big feelings could pass.

qa.q: How might Omkar's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel grateful that the teacher stayed calm and close with Omkar.

grounding: It illustrates a teacher kneeling, saying you are upset, I am here, moving objects aside and waiting quietly, which shows big feelings are survivable.

passage:
Monday. After his tantrum, Rishi sobbed. Tanuja started a lecture. He cried harder.
Wednesday. Rishi's crying turned to sobs. He held out his arms. Tanuja hugged him and gave him water. Zeenat didi breathed slowly beside them. Rishi's body got soft.
Friday. Rishi sobbed, then leaned into Tanuja on his own. She held him. He sipped water and sighed.

qa.q: What did Tanuja give Rishi on Wednesday?
qa.a: She gave him water after hugging him.

qa.q: What did Rishi want when he held out his arms?
qa.a: He wanted comfort and a hug, as his big feelings were settling.

qa.q: What did Tanuja learn between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: She learned that a lecture made it worse, while a hug, water and slow breathing helped Rishi settle.

qa.q: How might Zeenat didi see Rishi's change by Friday?
qa.a: She may notice he now leans in on his own, trusting that comfort will come.

grounding: It shows a toddler whose crying turns to sobs and who reaches out or leans in, needing a hug, water and slow breathing rather than a lecture.

passage: In their Bengaluru flat, Golu had been crying on the floor for a long time. Now the crying turned to small sobs. He lifted his arms toward Manjula. She picked him up and held him close. "Shh, shh." Devika Masi brought a small cup of water. Golu sipped, then leaned his head on Manjula's shoulder. She breathed slowly, and his breaths slowed too.

qa.a: Devika Masi brought him a small cup of water.

qa.q: What did Golu want when he lifted his arms?
qa.a: He needed comfort, wanting to be held after his big cry.

qa.q: What helped Golu's body settle?
qa.a: Being held close, a sip of water and Manjula's slow breathing helped him calm down, without any lecture.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel holding Golu?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and tender as his breathing slows. 😊

grounding: It illustrates a toddler whose crying becomes sobs, who reaches out to be held and settles with a hug, water and slow breaths.

subtype: Stage 6: Repair and naming the feeling [Response]
